text:
The Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Game expresses "grave reservations" about the Federal Government removing from the States "Their historic roles in the management of fish, wildlife and marine resources."

They continue, "It is our feeling that the States should retain a strong role in the management of rare and endangered species within its jurisdiction, and that the Secretary of Interior should allow the States to retain their historic roles in the management of fish, wildlife and marine resources."

They cite joint Federal-State management of the Atlantic salmon as a case of successful cooperation.
Indiana declines to endorse the proposed legislation because it provides for stronger Federal authority. The Department of Natural Resources feels that States are in the best position to determine which species are endangered. The Fish and Game Division objects to implication by the environment impact statement that the Federal Government could manage species "likely to become threatened." They "do not favor removing listed endangered species from the State's jurisdiction, but feel Federal assistance may be warranted in some circumstances."
The Nebraska Game and Parks Commission points out that their State has enacted laws "to comply with and be consistent with the intent of the Federal law, that of providing full protection to the threatened or endangered species of wildlife." They suggest Federal jurisdiction be imposed only when the State fails to enact legislation with the intent of the Federal law. Nebraska has approximately 45 conservation officers compared to three Federal enforcement agents to protect wildlife including endangered species.
